questions.q: 'Please turn ___ the volume — it is too loud.' (down) — where does 'it' go if we replace 'the volume'?
questions.a: 'turn it down' — pronouns must split separable phrasal verbs; 'turn down it' is illegal. A wrong answer 'turn down it' shows the pronoun rule missing.

questions.q: 'She ran ___ an old friend at the market.' into/across/after?
questions.a: 'into' — 'run into' = meet by chance; 'ran after' = chased. A wrong answer shows literal-particle reading instead of the fused meaning.

questions.q: Which is wrong: 'look after the baby' / 'look the baby after' / 'look after her'?
questions.a: 'look the baby after' — 'look after' is inseparable; the object follows the whole unit. Pronouns too: 'look after her' — inseparables never split even for pronouns.

questions.q: ______ matters: 'put off the meeting' / 'put the meeting off' both work, but pronouns force splitting — 'put it off', never 'put off it'.
Fill in the blank: Phrasal verbs fuse verb + ______ into a new meaning the parts don't predict: 'put off' = postpone, 'give in' = yield, 'look after' = care for.

Fill in the blank: The pronoun rule is the testable core: ______ phrasal verbs MUST split around pronouns — 'turn it down', 'pick her up', 'put it off' — while noun objects may split or stay together.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student interprets common phrasal verbs in context, applies the pronoun-splitting rule to separable verbs, and distinguishes literal from idiomatic particle meanings.
